name: Lacunol
subcategory: retrograde amnestic — targeted memory excision agent
manufacturer: Street synthesis — Shelf labs (formula believed stolen from Lazarus Pharmaceuticals R&D)
description: Lacunol is a targeted retrograde amnestic compound that disrupts hippocampal memory consolidation pathways and actively degrades recently encoded synaptic engrams, selectively erasing between one and seventy-two hours of memory depending on dosage. The compound interfaces with BCI memory-logging systems to simultaneously corrupt or delete the corresponding neural-link records, producing a clean gap in both organic and digital memory that reads as a technical fault rather than a deletion. Victims awaken with no awareness of the gap — they simply have no memory of the target period and believe they were asleep or unconscious.
effects: Retrograde memory erasure of 1-72 hours depending on dose
Simultaneous BCI log corruption — gap reads as hardware fault
Victim has no subjective awareness of missing time
Dose-titratable with reasonable precision at ±2 hour accuracy
side_effects: Imprecise erasure can bleed into adjacent memory, creating disturbing fragmentary gaps
Repeated use causes cumulative hippocampal damage and accelerated baseline memory degradation
Approximately 12% of subjects experience 'echo fragments' — intrusive partial sensory memories of the erased period that surface as dreams or déjà vu
BCI log corruption is detectable by forensic analysis — appears as fault but a skilled technician will recognize the pattern
duration: Amnestic effect is permanent for the targeted window; sedative effect lasts 4-8 hours
street_price: Φ600–Φ2,200 per dose (price scales with precision)
cultural_context: Lacunol is the cleanup tool — used after crimes, after secrets, after things that should not have been witnessed. On the Shelf it circulates as a rough instrument: witnesses get dosed and wake up not knowing what they saw. In higher tiers it's used more surgically — a corpo security team tidying up an incident, a fixer erasing a client's presence from a location. There's a grim irony in GLMZ's surveillance-saturated culture that the most effective privacy tool is a poison. Some people use it voluntarily on themselves, paying to erase traumatic experiences — an underground practice called 'clean slating' that underground therapists treat as a form of self-harm.
story_hooks: A Shelf kid wakes up with 14 hours missing and echo fragments that keep surfacing as nightmares — something red, something running, a face she doesn't recognize. Someone doesn't want her to remember what she saw.

A forensic BCI technician has developed an algorithm that can reconstruct the emotional residue of erased memories — not the content, but the shape of the feeling. She doesn't know yet that this makes her a target.

A fixer is hired to dose a witness but discovers the target has already been dosed by someone else — and the two missing windows don't overlap, which means there were two separate things that needed erasing.
